programme: REST (NRSF) repression of the canonical RE1/NRSE-bearing neuronal identity gene battery — among its listed targets this includes BDNF, GRIN2B, SYP, TUBB3, TH, TAC1, VIP, CARTPT, SCG2, UCHL1, NPPB, HTR1A, TPH2 — the same target set repeatedly recovered in genome-wide REST occupancy studies.
role_in_a: In Huntington's disease, wild-type huntingtin normally sequesters REST in the cytoplasm of neurons; mutant huntingtin loses this interaction, allowing REST to accumulate in the nucleus and silence its neuronal target genes (BDNF and the rest of this battery), a mechanism documented directly in HD cortex (PMID 42080424).
role_in_b: In lower-grade glioma, REST is reactivated to keep tumor cells away from a mature neuronal state, repressing the same identity-gene battery so cells remain in a less-differentiated, proliferative state; this has been studied directly as a REST regulatory network split by IDH mutation status (PMID 38711090).
shared_axis: Both diseases converge on the same REST-controlled gene set for opposite ends: HD pathology follows from losing neurons that need these genes switched on, glioma pathology follows from a tumor cell population that benefits from keeping them switched off. The shared axis is the RE1-silencing mechanism itself, not a shared clinical or anatomical relationship between the two diseases.
reasoning: REST's target list here matches the textbook RE1/NRSE gene set almost gene-for-gene, and each disease has a direct, disease-specific PMID placing REST's regulatory activity in it — but no retrieved source connects the two diseases to each other through REST, so that link is inference, not documentation. The other eleven factors contribute no usable evidence, so the account cannot lean on anything beyond REST alone.
support: PMID 42080424 — direct study of REST-associated developmental gene expression disruption in Huntington's disease cortex, places REST in disease A. PMID 38711090 — direct study of REST regulatory networks stratified by IDH status in glioma, places REST in disease B. Remaining PMIDs (SMAD7's 25983322/27574009 on TGF-β signaling, HEYL's 41602168, PRRX1's, MEOX1's, POU2AF1's, IRF4's) are either off-topic for their factor's disease or about a pathway unconnected to REST's programme, so none extend this account.
how_to_falsify: Knock down or CRISPRi-silence REST in an HD patient-derived neuronal (iPSC) model and separately in an IDH-mutant LGG line, then measure the shared target battery (BDNF, GRIN2B, SYP, TUBB3, TH). If de-repression fails in either model, or occurs without the expected phenotypic consequence (no rescue of neuronal markers in the HD model, no shift toward differentiation/reduced proliferation in the glioma model), the shared-axis account is wrong. A REST ChIP-seq/CUT&RUN comparison showing no occupancy at these loci in HD-relevant tissue or in LGG samples would also falsify it.
caveats: The HD network here is built from blood, not brain, while the LGG network is brain-derived; the cytoplasmic-sequestration mechanism linking mutant huntingtin to nuclear REST is documented in neurons, not blood cells, so this blood-derived concordance may reflect REST's ordinary baseline repression of neuronal genes in a non-neural tissue rather than HD-specific pathology — that gap is bridged by reasoning, not by anything retrieved. REST was concordant in 286 of 651 patient-group comparisons (44%, across 4 independent cohort pairs) — a real but non-majority fraction. The other eleven factors (immune: SP100, IRF4, POU2AF1, ZNF521; Notch/vascular: HEY2, HEYL; TGF-β/EMT/skeletal: SMAD7, PRRX1, MEOX1, SOX5, ZFPM2) returned essentially no relevant literature and do not extend or corroborate the REST programme; the account rests on REST alone. None of the single-view or tissue-generic exclusions belong to the REST neuronal-silencing programme, so their removal does not weaken this account.
